content: Contact tracing is an effective method to interrupt the transmission chain of the Ebola virus, but it must be initiated immediately upon identifying a suspected, probable, or confirmed case of Ebola. The identification of such cases, or deaths related to Ebola, should trigger an immediate alert system. Laboratory confirmation of the diagnosis should not delay the initiation of contact tracing. When a potential Ebola case is detected in a healthcare facility or community, a Case Investigation Team must be promptly mobilized to investigate. Contacts of the case include individuals who had direct physical contact with the patient (alive or deceased) during their illness. This includes those who touched the patient’s blood or bodily fluids (such as urine, feces, vomit, tears, or sweat). Sexual contacts, including unprotected intercourse with male survivors within 12 months of recovery (if their semen has not been tested or has not yet tested negative), are also considered contacts. Household members who lived with the patient since the onset of symptoms, individuals who touched the patient’s clothing or linens, and those who participated in burial preparation rituals or funerals where they had contact with the body or fluids are also considered contacts. Additionally, breastfeeding infants of infected mothers or survivors (if the breast milk has not been tested or converted to PCR-negative) are included. Patients discharged from Ebola Treatment Centers (ETCs) after negative PCR results within the last 21 days are also monitored. Healthcare workers who cared for the patient without proper Ebola precautions, including full personal protective equipment (PPE), and other patients in the same medical ward are considered contacts. This includes clinicians, aides, cleaners, waste management staff, and laboratory technicians. However, individuals who attended a safe burial (where the body was in a body bag and handled according to protocol) or attended without contact with the body or fluids are not considered contacts. If there is uncertainty, anyone who attended an unsafe burial should be reviewed as a potential contact. Asymptomatic contacts are not infectious. However, contacts admitted to hospitals for other illnesses should be screened for new Ebola symptoms during every shift. PCR testing is the gold standard for confirming Ebola cases. A positive PCR test confirms the presence of the virus. However, during the first three days of symptoms, PCR tests may yield false negatives, necessitating a second test on day three. If symptoms resolve before day three, a second test may not be required. In children, determining the onset of symptoms can be challenging, and repeat PCR testing is recommended for symptomatic children who are contacts. Newborns of mothers who are suspected or probable Ebola cases should be handled with full PPE, even if the initial PCR test is negative. Neonates born to confirmed Ebola cases should remain in the ETC and undergo repeat PCR testing if symptomatic. If asymptomatic, neonatal blood PCR should be tested on days 22 and 24 after birth. If both tests are negative, the neonate may be discharged with a feeding plan. Surveillance systems must ensure the completion of case investigation forms. Healthcare facilities should have a surveillance officer working with clinicians to complete these forms. If unavailable, clinicians must fill out the forms, assign a unique identification number or barcode, and notify the surveillance system. Families or next of kin should also be informed of the patient’s admission. All laboratory samples should be considered highly infectious. Early recognition of viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) like Ebola depends on a high index of clinical suspicion. Confirming the diagnosis requires specialized reference laboratories with biosafety infrastructure. Mobile laboratories near outbreak hotspots are essential for timely PCR testing. Personnel handling samples must be trained in proper PPE use and adhere to strict safety protocols. Samples must be appropriately labeled, triple-packaged, and transported to designated reference laboratories marked as “urgent” with biohazard signs. PCR testing detects viral RNA by amplifying its copies, with results reported as cycle threshold (Ct) values or viral load. Lower Ct values indicate higher viral loads. Diagnostic tests should be selected based on technical specifications, disease prevalence, and the implications of test results. Both PCR and automated PCR systems like GeneXpert are nucleic acid amplification tests and can confirm Ebola infection. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) with high specificity and sensitivity are recommended for screening in remote settings where PCR is inaccessible. However, RDT results must be confirmed by PCR. False-negative results may occur in early infection phases when viral levels are low. Negative PCR results within three days of symptom onset require repeat testing 2–3 days later. Oral swabs are less sensitive than blood PCR and are only taken from corpses with high viral loads. Patients presenting late in their illness or with mild disease may have cleared viremia and test PCR-negative. In such cases, serology can be used if clinical suspicion remains high. Laboratory diagnosis of VHFs like Ebola, Marburg, Lassa fever, or Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) can be challenging depending on the phase of illness and prior exposure. PCR is the preferred method for acute-phase diagnosis, while IgM and IgG antibody tests provide evidence of recent or past infections, respectively. Cross-reactivity can complicate IgG assays. Viral levels increase during the early days of symptoms, correlating with infectiousness. A strong immune response leads to antibody production (IgM and IgG), while a weak response correlates with high viral loads and increased mortality. For deceased patients, immunohistochemistry on post-mortem skin necropsy or PCR on oral swabs is used to confirm VHF. All clinical samples from suspected VHF patients should be processed as highly infectious and sent to designated laboratories. Essential laboratory tests should be conducted in dedicated VHF testing facilities to minimize exposure risks. False-negative results in early infection phases necessitate repeat testing. In cases of high clinical suspicion, testing for other VHFs like Lassa fever should be considered, especially if existing tests are negative.
